On the use of this particle, the discussion by H. Heller in Philologus vol. 8 p. 277-308 is worth reading. Agreeing with him for the most part, Baeumlein (Investigations on Greek Particles) p. 98 and Wehr, who collected Aristophanic examples in Quaestiones Aristophaneae I p. 51, observed that the varied use of this particle comes down to this: that some matter is indicated as evident, and the force either of the single word to which it is attached or of the whole sentence is emphasized. For it is not always joined to the primary word, which in the verses of poets was often not allowed by the meter. There is no Latin particle that corresponds to it everywhere, but there are several which can be used to interpret it according to the different nature of the passages, of which 'iam' is suitable for most. The opinion of some grammarians, mentioned by Eustathius p. 143, 22 and where he deals with writing νῦν δή [now indeed] as one word p. 174, that the particle when joined with certain other particles becomes enclitic, was groundless.
